content_html:
Digital Design and Manufacture

Computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacture have transformed how products move from concept to production. Computer-Aided Design (CAD) allows designers to model products precisely on-screen, test their appearance and function digitally, and generate the files needed to control manufacturing machinery. Computer-Aided Manufacture (CAM) takes those files and uses them to directly control machine tools, removing the need for a skilled operator to set up every cut or movement manually.

Together, CAD and CAM form a workflow that can take a product from initial sketch to finished part with very high precision and repeatability. This does not mean they replace skilled designers — the creativity and judgement of the designer remain essential — but they do change what skills are most valued in modern manufacturing.

Advantages of CAD

CAD software allows designers to create two-dimensional drawings and three-dimensional solid models that can be rotated, sectioned and rendered to look like the finished product. Changes to one dimension automatically update the whole model, eliminating the redrawing required in manual draughting. Designers can simulate how a structure will behave under load (Finite Element Analysis), check whether moving parts will clash before any physical prototype is made, and share files instantly with manufacturers or clients anywhere in the world.

CAD also enables rapid prototyping: a 3D model can be exported directly to a 3D printer or CNC machine within minutes of completion. The file is the product specification, reducing the chance of errors introduced by verbal or written instructions. Multiple iterations of a design can be tested digitally at almost no cost before expensive physical prototyping begins.

Key Fact

Key CAD advantages: designs can be modified instantly and shared globally; simulations can test structural performance before manufacture; files can be output directly to CAM machines, reducing manual error. Key disadvantage: high software cost and significant training time required before productivity improves.

Disadvantages of CAD

CAD software licences are expensive — professional packages such as AutoCAD or SolidWorks can cost thousands of pounds per seat per year. Hardware must be powerful enough to handle large assemblies without lag. Training staff to use CAD competently takes significant time, and there is a risk of over-reliance on the software: designers who cannot sketch or think in 3D without a computer lose problem-solving flexibility.

There is also a security risk: digital design files can be copied and shared, creating potential intellectual property problems. A factory that loses its server, or a design studio that is subject to a cyberattack, may lose access to years of design data if backup protocols are not in place.

Advantages of CAM

CAM-controlled machines can run 24 hours a day without rest, producing identical parts every cycle. This consistency is impossible to match with hand-operated tools, where operator fatigue introduces variation over time. Complex shapes that would take a skilled machinist hours to produce manually can be cut automatically from a CAD file. This is especially important for three-dimensional contoured surfaces in product design and for fine detail work in jewellery and signage.

CNC (computer numerical control) machines coordinate movement across multiple axes — typically X, Y and Z — to produce precise, complex geometries. Once programmed, a CNC machine can produce identical parts in batch quantities without further operator intervention. Waste is reduced because the toolpath can be optimised to minimise material removal.

Key Fact

CAM reduces waste in two ways: toolpaths can be optimised by software to minimise material removed (nesting patterns on sheet material), and the consistency of machine operation means fewer rejected parts due to operator error. This makes CAM particularly cost-effective for batch and mass production.

Disadvantages of CAM

CAM equipment has very high capital costs. A CNC milling machine or laser cutter suitable for industry costs tens of thousands of pounds. Set-up time is significant: programming the toolpath and fixturing the workpiece correctly requires skilled technicians. For one-off or very small batch production, the time and cost of set-up may exceed the time it would take a skilled craftsperson to make the part manually.

When a CAM machine breaks down, production stops entirely unless a spare machine is available — a single point of failure that does not exist in a workshop where multiple skilled workers can redistribute tasks. Maintenance requires specialist engineers who command high salaries.

CNC Routing and Laser Cutting

CNC routing uses a rotating bit to cut, carve and shape flat sheet materials — typically wood, MDF, acrylic and soft metals. The router head moves across the bed following the CAD file toolpath. It is widely used in furniture manufacture, signage and architectural models. CNC routing can produce complex interlocking joints and relief carving that would be impractical by hand in batch quantities.

Laser cutting uses a focused beam of high-energy light to cut or engrave flat sheet materials with extreme precision. Acrylic, wood, card, fabric and thin sheet metal can all be cut without physical contact, meaning no blade wear and no cutting forces that might distort delicate pieces. The kerf (cut width) is typically less than 0.5 mm. Laser cutting is used in schools and small workshops for model-making, in industry for precision sheet metal parts, and in the jewellery and fashion industries for intricate fabric and leather cutting. A significant advantage is the ability to nest many parts tightly on one sheet, minimising material waste.

CNC embroidery and vinyl cutting extend CAM principles to textiles and graphics: embroidery machines follow a digitised pattern to stitch designs into fabric precisely and repeatedly; vinyl cutters trace vector paths to cut self-adhesive vinyl for signage, vehicle graphics and garment decoration. Both processes produce consistent, high-quality results at speeds impossible to match by hand.

3D Printing (Additive Manufacturing)

3D printing builds parts by adding material layer by layer, rather than removing material as CNC machines do. The most common process is Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM): a thermoplastic filament (typically PLA or ABS) is heated and extruded through a nozzle, depositing each layer on the build platform until the part is complete. This allows complex internal geometries — hollow sections, internal channels — that are impossible to produce by subtractive machining.

Other processes include Stereolithography (SLA), which cures liquid resin with a UV laser to build very fine-detail parts, and Selective Laser Sintering (SLS), which fuses polymer or metal powder with a laser and is suitable for production-grade engineering parts without support material. Airbus uses metal SLS to produce titanium brackets and connectors for aircraft cabins — components that would be difficult and wasteful to machine from solid billet.

Advantages: complex geometries at no extra tooling cost; no fixed tooling means economical one-off production; rapid iteration of design without new moulds; can produce personalised or bespoke parts directly from a digital file. Disadvantages: slow build speed compared with injection moulding for large batches; FDM parts have visible layer lines and may require surface finishing; material choice is narrower than conventional manufacturing; parts may be weaker along the layer boundaries than in the in-plane direction (anisotropic strength).

Students sometimes describe ‘CAD’ when they mean the machine cutting the part, or ‘CAM’ when they mean the drawing software. Keep them distinct: CAD is the design tool (the computer screen, the modelling software, the drawing or simulation); CAM is the manufacturing tool (the CNC machine, the laser cutter, the 3D printer). The CAD file is the input; the CAM process is the output. For exam questions, specify both the design tool and the manufacturing machine — e.g. ‘the designer creates the part in CAD software, then outputs a DXF file to a laser cutter (CAM) which cuts the acrylic sheet.’

lesson_title: Electronic Systems and the Input-Process-Output Model
content_html:
How Electronic Systems Work

Electronic systems are at the heart of almost every modern product — from a bedside lamp that dims automatically to a fire alarm that wakes a building. Rather than thinking about individual wires and components, designers use a systems approach to plan how a product will function. This means dividing any electronic product into three linked stages: input, process and output. Understanding this model is essential for answering questions about how electronic products detect, decide and respond.

The Input–Process–Output Model

The input–process–output (IPO) model describes all electronic systems. The three stages always occur in this sequence:

  • Input — a sensor or switch detects a change in the environment and converts it into an electrical signal. Examples include a light-dependent resistor detecting low light, or a microswitch being pressed by a moving part.
  • Process — a processor (such as a transistor circuit or microcontroller) receives the signal and decides what to do. It may compare the input against a set threshold and trigger a response only when a condition is met.
  • Output — the system produces a visible, audible or physical response. Common output devices include LEDs, buzzers, motors and display screens.
Key Fact

Every electronic system has three stages: input (sensor detects a change), process (circuit or microcontroller decides) and output (device responds). No electronic product exists that skips one of these stages.

Input Sensors

Sensors are the ‘senses’ of an electronic system. They convert a physical change in the environment into a changing electrical signal. The most commonly tested sensors are:

  • Light-dependent resistor (LDR) — its resistance is high in darkness and falls as light intensity increases. A street lamp controller uses an LDR so the lamp switches on at dusk and off at dawn.
  • Thermistor — a thermistor has high resistance at low temperatures and low resistance when warm. A central heating thermostat uses a thermistor to detect when the room drops below the set temperature.
  • Microswitch — a mechanical switch with a small lever; a tiny force triggers it. Printers use microswitches to detect when a paper tray is open.
  • Moisture sensor — two conductive tracks separated by a gap; when water bridges the gap, current flows, completing the circuit. A plant-watering alert uses this type. Important: simply naming “moisture sensor” is not enough in the exam — you must explain that water completes the circuit between the two tracks, changing the current flowing to the processor.

Sensors produce either analogue or digital signals. An analogue signal varies continuously — the output of a thermistor changes smoothly as temperature rises. A digital signal is either on or off: a microswitch is either pressed (1) or not pressed (0). Most microcontrollers work in the digital domain, so analogue signals from sensors like LDRs are converted using an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) before the processor can act on them.

Understanding this distinction matters for exam questions asking you to explain how a sensor interfaces with a microcontroller. A thermistor gives a continuously varying voltage; the ADC samples this many times per second and converts each sample into a binary number the processor can compare against a stored threshold value.

Output Devices

The output stage converts the electrical signal back into a physical form the user can see, hear or feel:

  • LED (light-emitting diode) — emits light when current flows in the correct direction. Used as indicator lights, display digits and, increasingly, as the primary light source in products such as cycle lamps.
  • Buzzer — converts electrical pulses into sound via a vibrating disc. Common in alarms, timers and door entry systems.
  • Motor — converts electrical energy into rotary motion. Used to move conveyor belts, open automatic doors and drive robotic arms.
  • Relay — an electromagnetic switch allowing a low-current circuit to control a high-current device safely, such as a microcontroller switching a mains-voltage motor.
Key Fact

An LDR has high resistance in darkness and low resistance in bright light — the opposite of what many students expect. A thermistor has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot. Getting these directions wrong is the most common error in sensor questions.

Block Diagrams and Circuit Diagrams

Designers use two main types of diagram to represent electronic systems:

  • Block diagram — shows the function of each stage as a labelled box connected by arrows. It does not show individual components or wiring. A block diagram for a security light might show: [LDR] → [Processor] → [LED array].
  • Circuit diagram — shows every component using standard British Standard (BS) symbols and the wiring between them. More detailed than a block diagram and used by engineers building the product.

A basic IPO system runs in one direction: input → process → output. A more advanced system uses feedback to make the output self-correcting. In a closed-loop system, the output is monitored and compared to a desired value; any difference (error) is used to adjust the process. A central heating system is a classic example: the thermistor measures room temperature (feedback), the controller compares it to the target, and the boiler fires or cuts off accordingly.

In contrast, an open-loop system has no feedback: a toaster with only a timer heats for a fixed period regardless of whether the bread is actually toasted. Open-loop systems are simpler and cheaper but less accurate. Closed-loop systems cost more but respond dynamically to changing conditions, making them preferable in safety-critical applications such as industrial robots and medical devices.

Flowcharts

A flowchart maps the logical steps in a control system. Standard shapes are used: ovals for start/stop, rectangles for process steps, diamonds for decisions (with yes/no branches). A flowchart for an automatic night-light would show: Start → Is it dark? (No → loop back; Yes → Turn LED on) → loop back to check again. Flowcharts are particularly useful for describing how a programmable component such as a microcontroller responds to sensor inputs.

Why Use Programmable Components?

Traditional electronic circuits are designed to do one thing. Change the task and you change the circuit — which means redesigning the hardware and going back to manufacture. Programmable components solve this problem. They allow engineers to change what a circuit does simply by loading a different program, with no change to the physical components. This makes products cheaper to develop, easier to update and more versatile — a significant commercial advantage for any manufacturer.

Microcontrollers and PICs

The most important type of programmable component in GCSE Design and Technology is the microcontroller. A microcontroller contains:

  • A processor (CPU) — executes the instructions in the program, performing calculations and making decisions.
  • Memory — stores the program (in non-volatile flash memory, so it survives power loss) and temporary working data (in RAM).
  • Input/output (I/O) pins — connect to sensors, switches, LEDs, motors and other peripheral devices. Pins can be individually configured as inputs or outputs.

A PIC (Programmable Interface Controller) is a popular family of microcontroller chip. PICs are small, low-cost and low-power, making them ideal for embedding in consumer products such as washing machines, microwave ovens and children’s toys. A PIC is programmed by writing code on a computer and then uploading it to the chip via a programmer device.

Key Fact

A microcontroller contains a processor, memory and I/O pins on a single chip. It can read sensor inputs, make decisions according to its program, and control output devices — replacing a large number of separate electronic components with a single programmable unit.

Interfacing with Inputs and Outputs

A microcontroller sits at the process stage of the input–process–output model. It interfaces with input sensors and output devices via its I/O pins:

  • Input interfacing — a sensor (LDR, thermistor, microswitch) connects to an input pin. The microcontroller reads the voltage at that pin and compares it to a threshold in its program. For analogue sensors, an internal analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) converts the continuously varying voltage to a number the processor can use.
  • Output interfacing — output pins switch devices on or off. Because a microcontroller’s output pins can only supply small currents (typically 20–40 mA), high-power devices such as motors must be controlled via a transistor or relay, which acts as a switch that the microcontroller triggers.

Programs running on microcontrollers are made more efficient using sub-routines. Instead of writing the same sequence of instructions every time a task is needed, the programmer writes the instructions once as a sub-routine and calls it whenever required. For example, a “sound alarm” sub-routine that pulses a buzzer three times could be called from many different points in the program — when temperature exceeds a limit, when a door opens, or when a battery runs low — without rewriting the buzzer code each time.

A macro is a shorthand label assigned to a frequently used sequence of instructions. In block-based or flow-chart programming environments (common in schools), macros allow students to group a set of actions under one name and use it as a single step. Both sub-routines and macros reduce the length and complexity of programs, making them easier to test, debug and modify.

Benefits of Reprogrammable Systems

The ability to reprogram a microcontroller after the product is assembled brings several practical advantages that examiners expect students to explain with product context:

  • Flexibility — the same hardware can be used in different products simply by changing the program. A manufacturer can produce one PCB design and program it differently for a bedroom alarm clock and a kitchen timer.
  • Firmware updates — faults discovered after a product ships can be corrected by updating the program over a network or via a USB connection, without recalling and physically modifying the hardware.
  • Reduced component count — one microcontroller replaces many discrete components (comparators, counters, timers), reducing board size, material cost and assembly time.
  • Faster prototyping — engineers can write, test and refine the control logic rapidly without soldering new components. This shortens the development cycle and reduces waste.
Key Fact

Programmable systems can be updated after manufacture by changing the software, with no change to the physical circuit. This is a major commercial advantage: it reduces tooling costs, enables bug fixes without product recalls, and allows one hardware design to serve multiple product variants.

Limitations of Programmable Components

Microcontrollers are not always the best choice. Students must be able to evaluate both sides:

  • Programming expertise required — writing reliable control software demands skill. Bugs in the code can cause dangerous malfunctions in safety-critical products.
  • Higher unit cost for simple tasks — for a product that only ever needs to do one thing (such as a simple on/off switch), a fixed resistor-transistor circuit is cheaper and more reliable than a microcontroller.
  • Power consumption — a microcontroller consumes more power than a simple passive circuit, which matters in battery-powered products where runtime is critical.
  • Software dependency — if the program is corrupted (e.g. by a power surge during programming), the product fails entirely. A purely hardware circuit has no software to corrupt.

Microcontrollers are embedded in a huge range of everyday products. A modern washing machine uses a microcontroller to time wash cycles, monitor water temperature via a thermistor, detect an unbalanced drum via an accelerometer, and control the motor speed — all in a single chip. Without reprogrammability, manufacturers would need to produce different circuit boards for each wash programme (delicates, cottons, quick wash) instead of a single board with different software settings.

In Design and Technology projects, PICs are commonly programmed using block-based visual environments such as Flowcode or PicAxe BASIC. These tools generate machine code from a visual flowchart or simple text commands, making programming accessible without requiring advanced software engineering skills. The logic the student builds in the flowchart maps directly onto the sub-routine structure described in this lesson.

lesson_title: Mechanical Devices and Types of Motion
content_html:
Motion in Mechanical Systems

Mechanical systems convert one type of motion into another, or change the direction and magnitude of a force. Understanding the four types of motion is fundamental to analysing how any mechanism works — from a bicycle gearset to an industrial press. Before examining specific devices, you need to recognise and describe each motion type accurately, as exam questions often ask students to identify which motion is produced at a given point in a mechanism.

The Four Types of Motion

Rotary motion is circular movement around a fixed axis. Gears, wheels and motors all produce rotary motion. It is the most common type in powered machines because electric motors naturally produce rotation.

Linear motion is movement in a straight line. A drawer sliding in a cabinet, a piston being pushed along a cylinder, or a rack gear moving along a track are all examples of linear motion. Many mechanisms exist specifically to convert rotary motion (from a motor) into linear motion useful for the product’s function.

Reciprocating motion is backwards-and-forwards movement in a straight line. A jigsaw blade, a sewing machine needle and the pistons in a car engine all move with reciprocating motion. Reciprocating motion is often produced by converting rotary motion using a crank and slider mechanism.

Oscillating motion is a swinging or rocking movement — similar to reciprocating but following an arc rather than a straight line. A pendulum, a metronome and the escapement mechanism in a mechanical clock all exhibit oscillating motion.

Key Fact

The four types of motion are: rotary (circular), linear (straight line, one direction), reciprocating (straight line, back and forth) and oscillating (arc, back and forth). Distinguishing reciprocating from oscillating — both go ‘back and forth’ but reciprocating is along a straight line while oscillating follows a curved path — is a common exam trap.

Levers

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots about a fixed point called the fulcrum. Levers change the magnitude (size) of a force or its direction. The three classes of lever are defined by the positions of the effort, fulcrum and load:

  • First-order lever — fulcrum between effort and load. Changes direction of force. A seesaw and a pair of scissors are first-order levers.
  • Second-order lever — load between fulcrum and effort. Multiplies force (mechanical advantage > 1). A wheelbarrow is a second-order lever: the axle is the fulcrum, the load sits in the barrow, and the effort is applied at the handles.
  • Third-order lever — effort between fulcrum and load. Sacrifices force to gain speed or range of movement. Tweezers and a fishing rod are third-order levers.

A linkage is a set of rigid bars connected by pivots. Linkages transmit and transform motion within a mechanism. A reverse motion linkage has a fixed pivot in the centre of a bar; when one end moves up, the other moves down — used in bell-crank mechanisms and some vehicle steering systems. A parallel motion linkage keeps a bar horizontal as it moves, used in drawing boards, architect’s parallel rulers and pantograph mechanisms.

Linkages are lightweight, strong and simple to manufacture. They appear frequently in mechanisms that must redirect motion without the complexity of gears or electronics.

Gear Systems

Gears are toothed wheels that mesh together to transmit rotary motion. They change speed, torque (turning force) and direction of rotation. The gear attached to the driving source (motor) is the driver gear; the gear it turns is the driven gear. The teeth on meshing gears must be the same size.

Key relationships in gear systems:

  • A large driven gear turns slower than the driver but with more torque — useful for lifting heavy loads (clock mechanisms, winches).
  • A small driven gear turns faster than the driver but with less torque — useful for speed (fan blades, model racing cars).
  • Two meshing gears rotate in opposite directions. An idler gear placed between them makes the driven gear rotate in the same direction as the driver.

A rack and pinion converts rotary motion to linear motion. The circular pinion gear meshes with a flat toothed rack; as the pinion rotates, the rack slides in a straight line. Car steering systems, adjustable office chairs and the quill on a pillar drill all use rack-and-pinion mechanisms.

Bevel gears have angled teeth and mesh at right angles (or other angles), changing the axis of rotation by 90°. A hand-powered drill uses bevel gears to convert horizontal handle rotation into vertical drill rotation.

A worm drive has a helical screw (worm) meshing with a worm gear. The worm can only drive the gear — the gear cannot back-drive the worm — making this ideal for self-locking mechanisms such as guitar tuning pegs. Worm drives produce very high gear ratios in a compact space.

Cams and Followers

A cam is an off-centre rotating disc. A follower rests on the cam’s surface and rises and falls as the cam rotates, converting rotary motion into reciprocating or oscillating motion. Cam shape determines the follower’s movement pattern:

  • Snail (drop) cam — produces a slow rise followed by a sudden drop. Used in escapements and alarm mechanisms.
  • Eccentric (circular offset) cam — produces a smooth, regular rise and fall. Used in engine valve systems.
  • Pear-shaped cam — produces a long dwell (pause) at top and bottom, with rapid rise and fall. Used in sewing machines to control the needle action.
Key Fact

The rack and pinion converts rotary to linear motion. A cam and follower converts rotary to reciprocating motion. Gears and pulleys transmit and modify rotary motion without changing its type. Being able to state the motion conversion is a one-mark gain in most exam questions on mechanisms.

Pulley Systems

Pulleys use a belt or chain running over one or more grooved wheels to transmit rotary motion over a distance. Unlike gears (which mesh directly), pulleys rely on friction between the belt and the pulley groove to transmit force. This means friction is required for the mechanism to work — a common misconception is that friction is always undesirable. Without sufficient friction, the belt slips and power is lost. Pulley systems are widely used to transmit drive from motors to conveyor belts, lathes and washing machine drums.

lesson_title: Mechanical Calculations: Levers, Gears and Pulleys
content_html:
Why Calculations Matter in Mechanisms

Mechanical calculations allow engineers to predict exactly how much force a lever can generate, how fast a driven gear will spin, or how many times a pulley system multiplies an effort. In the exam, calculation questions require you to state the formula, substitute values and give a numerical answer with correct units — a formula alone scores zero. This lesson works through each calculation type fully before you practise, following the same method every time.

Mechanical Advantage

Mechanical advantage (MA) tells us how much a mechanism multiplies a force. A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the mechanism amplifies the effort; less than 1 means the mechanism sacrifices force to gain speed or range.

The formula is:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$$

For levers, MA can also be calculated from distances if force values are not given:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{distance from fulcrum to effort}}{\text{distance from fulcrum to load}}$$

A first-order lever has its fulcrum 0.2 m from the load and 0.8 m from the effort. Calculate the mechanical advantage.

Step 1 — Write the formula:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{distance from fulcrum to effort}}{\text{distance from fulcrum to load}}$$

Step 2 — Substitute values:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{0.8}{0.2}$$

Step 3 — Calculate and state answer:

$$\text{MA} = 4$$

The lever has a mechanical advantage of 4. This means an effort of 5 N would lift a load of 20 N. Note: MA has no units — it is a pure ratio.

The Principle of Moments

The principle of moments states that for a lever in equilibrium (balanced), the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment. A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot.

$$\text{Moment} = \text{Force} \times \text{perpendicular distance from pivot}$$

Units: Newton-metres (Nm). Force is in newtons (N) and distance is in metres (m).

A uniform lever is balanced on a fulcrum. A 60 N load sits 0.3 m from the fulcrum on the left. What effort must be applied 0.9 m from the fulcrum on the right to keep the lever balanced?

Step 1 — Write the principle of moments:

$$\text{Clockwise moment} = \text{Anticlockwise moment}$$

Step 2 — Substitute:

$$\text{Effort} \times 0.9 = 60 \times 0.3$$

Step 3 — Solve:

$$\text{Effort} = \frac{60 \times 0.3}{0.9} = \frac{18}{0.9} = 20 \text{ N}$$

An effort of 20 N is required. The lever gives a mechanical advantage of 3 (60 ÷ 20), confirming the longer effort arm tripled the force.

Key Fact

Moment (Nm) = Force (N) × perpendicular distance from pivot (m). The longer the effort arm, the smaller the effort needed to balance a given load — this is why a long spanner undoes a tight bolt more easily than a short one.

Gear Ratio

The gear ratio compares the number of teeth on the driven gear to those on the driver gear:

$$\text{Gear ratio} = \frac{\text{teeth on driven gear}}{\text{teeth on driver gear}}$$

A driver gear has 12 teeth. The driven gear has 48 teeth. The driver turns at 200 rpm. Calculate the gear ratio and the output speed of the driven gear.

Step 1 — Gear ratio:

$$\text{Gear ratio} = \frac{48}{12} = 4:1$$

Step 2 — Output speed:

$$\text{Output speed} = \frac{\text{Input speed}}{\text{Gear ratio}} = \frac{200}{4} = 50 \text{ rpm}$$

The driven gear turns at 50 rpm — four times slower than the driver, but with four times the torque. A 4:1 ratio is described as a step-down (reduction) gear. Always include units (rpm) in your final answer.

Velocity Ratio of Pulley Systems

In a belt-and-pulley system, the velocity ratio (VR) compares pulley diameters. Because both pulleys share the same belt, the belt travels at the same linear speed at both pulleys:

$$\text{VR} = \frac{\text{diameter of driven pulley}}{\text{diameter of driver pulley}}$$

The output speed of the driven pulley is:

$$\text{Output speed} = \frac{\text{Input speed}}{\text{VR}}$$

A motor drives a 50 mm diameter pulley (driver) connected by a belt to a 200 mm diameter pulley (driven). The motor runs at 1 200 rpm. Calculate the velocity ratio and output speed.

Step 1 — Velocity ratio:

$$\text{VR} = \frac{200}{50} = 4$$

Step 2 — Output speed:

$$\text{Output speed} = \frac{1200}{4} = 300 \text{ rpm}$$

The driven pulley turns at 300 rpm. As with gears, a larger driven pulley gives a slower but more powerful (higher torque) output. Remember: for this to work, the belt must not slip — friction between belt and pulley is essential.

Key Fact

Gear ratio and pulley velocity ratio both use the same structure: driven ÷ driver. A ratio greater than 1 means the output is slower with more torque (step-down). A ratio less than 1 means the output is faster with less torque (step-up). Always state the formula, show working, and include units in the final answer.

Forces in Structures and Products

Every physical product experiences forces during its use — the weight of books compresses a shelf, a twisted door handle experiences torsion, and a loaded bridge beam bends under traffic. Designers must understand the nature of these forces so they can choose the right material, shape and reinforcement strategy to ensure the product survives its intended service life without failing. Exam questions on this topic expect you to identify the type of stress acting on a component and justify a reinforcement choice with material and structural reasoning.

The Five Types of Stress

Tension is a pulling or stretching force. When two forces act along the same axis in opposite directions, pulling the material apart, the material is in tension. Examples: a rope suspending a load, a chain on a bicycle, the bottom flange of a loaded beam.

Compression is a pushing or squeezing force. When two forces act along the same axis pushing towards each other, the material is compressed and tends to shorten or buckle. Examples: the legs of a chair supporting a seated person, the columns of a building, the top flange of a loaded beam.

Torsion is a twisting force. When one end of a component is held fixed and a torque is applied to the other end, the material twists. A screwdriver shaft, a car drive shaft and a door handle spindle all experience torsion in normal use.

Shear is a cutting or sliding force where adjacent sections of a material tend to slide past each other. Scissors, chisels and bolts connecting structural members all experience shear. Shear is also the stress that causes a beam to fail by cracking vertically near its supports.

Bending occurs when a force acts perpendicular to the long axis of a component, causing it to curve. The top of a bent beam is in compression; the bottom is in tension. A shelf loaded at its centre, a diving board and a roof rafter all experience bending.

Key Fact

The five stresses are: tension (pulling apart), compression (pushing together), torsion (twisting), shear (sliding/cutting) and bending (top compressed, bottom stretched). A beam under a central load experiences both compression (top) and tension (bottom) simultaneously — this is a common exam question.

Reinforcement Methods by Material

Reinforcement increases a component’s resistance to failure without making it excessively heavy or expensive. Different material families use different structural techniques:

Papers and Boards

Corrugating paper creates a wavy internal layer that vastly increases bending stiffness. Corrugated cardboard packaging uses this principle: the fluted inner layer resists compression from the top surface, while the flat outer liners resist tension and provide a smooth printing surface. Without the corrugation, the same amount of paper would buckle under a fraction of the load.

Timbers

Laminating layers of wood (as in plywood or laminated veneer lumber) with the grain alternated at 90° distributes forces in multiple directions. A single piece of timber is strong along the grain but weak across it; plywood resists forces in both directions equally. Gussets — triangular corner reinforcements — are used at frame joints to resist racking (shear forces that push a rectangular frame into a parallelogram).

Metals

Metal sections can be formed into shapes that increase their second moment of area — effectively concentrating material away from the neutral axis to maximise resistance to bending. An I-beam (universal beam) is the classic example: the flanges are far from the centre, giving very high bending resistance with minimal material. Ribs on metal enclosures (such as those on the inside of cast aluminium gear housings) perform the same function, resisting bending while keeping the wall thin and light. Hollow box sections resist both bending and torsion more efficiently than solid sections of the same mass.

Polymers

Polymers are often reinforced at points of weakness using additional wall thickness, ribbing on the inside of moulded parts, or by embedding them in a matrix of fibres. Ribs on the inside of an injection-moulded plastic casing resist bending without increasing the outer wall thickness (which would cause sink marks and extend cooling time). Glass-reinforced polymer (GRP) uses glass fibres within a polyester resin matrix; the fibres resist tension that the resin alone could not withstand.

When a beam bends, stress is highest at the top (compression) and bottom (tension) surfaces and nearly zero at the neutral axis in the middle. An I-beam exploits this by placing the majority of its material at the flanges (top and bottom), where stress is highest, and using only a thin web in the middle where stress is low. The same mass of steel in a rectangular section would be far weaker in bending because much of the material sits near the neutral axis doing little structural work.

This principle also explains why hollow tubes resist bending and torsion better than solid rods of the same cross-sectional area: material near the centre contributes little to resisting these forces. Bicycle frames use aluminium or carbon fibre tubes for exactly this reason — light, stiff and strong because the material is distributed at the outer surface where stresses are highest.

Textiles and Fibres

Interfacing is a woven or non-woven fabric bonded to the reverse of a textile to add stiffness — used in shirt collars, waistbands and the structured panels of bags. Webbing — tightly woven strips of nylon, polyester or polypropylene — is used for straps and harnesses because it has very high tensile strength along its length. Quilting (sandwiching insulation between fabric layers, held by stitching) resists delamination and maintains the insulating layer’s thickness under repeated compression.

Key Fact

Reinforcement works by distributing stress over a larger area or redirecting it into a form the material can withstand. Corrugating (paper/boards), laminating (timber), ribbing and I-section profiles (metals), ribbing inside moulded parts (polymers) and interfacing/webbing (textiles) are all exam-required reinforcement techniques. Know at least one technique per material family.

The most common error in exam answers on this topic is confusing bending with compression. A shelf that sags in the middle is bending, not simply compressing — the top surface is in compression and the bottom is in tension. Stating only “the shelf is compressed by the books” misses the structure of the stress and will only score partial marks.

A second common error is describing reinforcement too vaguely. “Make it thicker” is not a reinforcement technique — it simply adds material without changing the distribution of stress. A specific answer names the structural form: “adding ribs to the inside of the moulded casing increases bending stiffness without increasing wall thickness, avoiding sink marks in the surface finish.” This level of specificity is required for the top mark band on applied questions.

From Wood Pulp to Printed Page

Paper and board are among the oldest industrial materials, yet they remain central to modern design—from product packaging to architectural models. Both begin as wood pulp, produced either mechanically (grinding logs into fibres) or chemically (using reagents to dissolve lignin and release clean cellulose). Chemical pulp produces stronger, longer-lasting sheets; mechanical pulp is cheaper but yellows over time because lignin remains in the fibres.

Paper is measured in two ways. Grammage (gsm) describes mass per unit area. Copy paper is typically 80 gsm; a premium business card may be 350 gsm. Microns describe physical thickness: standard copy paper sits around 100 microns. The two figures usually move together, but coated papers can be heavier per micron than uncoated ones because the coating adds density without adding much bulk.

Key Fact

Paper weight is measured in gsm (grams per square metre); paper thickness is measured in microns. Standard copy paper is around 80 gsm and approximately 100 microns thick. Card and board start at roughly 200 gsm.

ISO Paper Sizes

The international standard for paper sizing is the ISO 216 series. The A-series is built on a single mathematical relationship: each size is exactly half the area of the one above it, and the aspect ratio remains constant at 1:√2 (approximately 1:1.414). This means an A3 sheet folded in half gives two A4 sheets, an A4 folded in half gives two A5 sheets, and so on. A0 has an area of exactly 1 m². Designers use this relationship routinely when scaling artwork: an image laid out on A3 will reproduce correctly at A4 without distortion.

The B-series covers intermediate sizes (useful for posters and passports), and the C-series is used for envelopes (a C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet flat). In practice, the A-series is what designers, printers and students encounter daily.

The most commonly used A-series sizes in design and education:

SizeDimensions (mm)Typical use
A0841 × 1189Large posters, architectural drawings
A1594 × 841Exhibition posters, flip chart pads
A2420 × 594Technical drawings, display boards
A3297 × 420Design sheets, presentation boards
A4210 × 297Letters, standard printing
A5148 × 210Leaflets, notebooks
A6105 × 148Postcards, pocket notebooks

Types of Paper

Layout paper is thin and slightly translucent—ideal for developing ideas quickly in pencil. Designers layer sheets over earlier sketches to refine forms without starting from scratch. Tracing paper is more transparent still, used to copy existing drawings accurately. Cartridge paper is the general-purpose drawing paper used in most D&T studios: heavier than layout paper (typically 100–140 gsm), with a slightly textured surface that holds pencil and ink well. Bleed-proof paper has an extra smooth coating that stops alcohol-based markers bleeding through to the sheet beneath.

Recycled paper is made from post-consumer waste fibres that have been de-inked and re-pulped. Each recycling cycle shortens the fibres slightly, which reduces strength over successive cycles, but modern paper can contain 100% recycled content for many applications. Recycled paper typically has a slightly grey or cream tint rather than the bright white of virgin-fibre sheets, because optical brightening agents (OBAs) are harder to apply uniformly to recycled pulp.

Types of Board

Boards are heavier-duty sheets, generally above 200 gsm, produced by laminating multiple paper layers together or using a thicker single-ply process. The main boards used in GCSE D&T are:

  • Corrugated board—a sandwich of flat liners bonded to a fluted inner layer. The fluting creates a rigid structure that is surprisingly light. Used in protective transit packaging and models. Typically 3 mm to 5 mm thick but weighs far less than solid card of the same thickness.
  • Folding boxboard (FBB)—a multi-layer board with a white coated surface ideal for high-quality printing. Used in cereal boxes, medicine packets and cosmetic packaging. The inner layers may contain mechanical pulp to reduce cost, with a chemical-pulp surface layer for printability.
  • Mounting board—a thick, rigid board (1.5–3 mm) used to mount and present artwork or photographs. Available in many colours. Commonly used by designers to present rendered illustrations or to produce scale architectural models.
Key Fact

Corrugated board achieves rigidity through its fluted inner layer sandwiched between flat liners. Folding boxboard (FBB) is the standard for printed retail packaging. Mounting board is rigid presentation-quality board used to display artwork and build scale models.

Laminating and Finishing

Laminating applies a thin plastic film (typically polypropylene) to a printed sheet. Gloss laminate intensifies colour and reflects light; matt laminate reduces glare and gives a softer feel. Both significantly improve the product’s resistance to moisture, tearing and everyday handling. Laminating is common on book covers, loyalty cards and food packaging where the printed surface must survive repeated handling.

Other finishes include spot UV varnish (a glossy coating applied to specific areas only to create contrast), embossing (pressing a design into the board to create a raised surface) and foil blocking (applying a metallic foil under heat and pressure). Each adds cost and requires specialist equipment, but can significantly increase the perceived quality of a product.

The 12-mark extended response question asks you to demonstrate depth in ONE chosen material area. For papers and boards, top-band answers include: specific named paper or board types (not just “cardboard”), precise properties linked to application (e.g. folding boxboard’s coated surface enables high-quality litho printing for retail packaging), and at least one sustainability point (e.g. recycled content, biodegradable vs laminated boards at end of life). The weakest answers say “card is strong and light” without naming a specific board type or linking properties to a product context.

A strong Q6 paragraph on papers and boards might read: “Folding boxboard is used for cereal packaging because its multi-layer construction combines a smooth, coated outer surface for litho printing with mechanical-pulp inner layers that reduce cost. At end of life, unlaminated FBB is recyclable and biodegradable, making it preferable to plastics for mass-market retail packaging.” Note: three specific facts, a process link, and an environmental evaluation in one short paragraph.

Timber in Design and Industry

Timber is one of the most versatile structural materials available to designers, and the most popular choice for the in-depth extended response question in the written exam. Understanding the difference between hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards—and knowing named examples of each—is essential. The distinction begins at the tree: hardwoods come from deciduous trees (broad-leaved, generally slow-growing), while softwoods come from coniferous trees (evergreen, needle-leaved, generally faster-growing).

Importantly, “hardwood” and “softwood” are botanical classifications, not descriptions of physical hardness. Balsa—which is famously soft to the touch—is technically a hardwood because it comes from a deciduous tree. Conversely, some conifers produce surprisingly dense timber.

Key Fact

Hardwoods come from deciduous (broad-leaved) trees; softwoods come from coniferous (needle-leaved) trees. The terms describe botanical classification, not physical hardness. Balsa is a hardwood despite being soft; some conifers produce dense timber.

Named Hardwoods

The following hardwoods are named in the specification and are likely to appear in exam questions:

  • Oak—a dense, strong hardwood with an attractive grain and excellent durability. Used in furniture, flooring, wine barrels and construction. Oak can be finished naturally or stained; it reacts with iron fixings (producing dark stains), so stainless or brass fixings are preferred.
  • Beech—a pale, fine-grained hardwood that is very hard and resistant to splitting. Commonly used in furniture (especially chair seats and legs), tool handles and children’s toys. Beech machines and sands very cleanly.
  • Mahogany—a medium-density tropical hardwood with a rich reddish-brown colour and an interlocking grain that resists warping. Traditional choice for furniture, interior joinery and boat building. Sustainability concerns exist around tropical hardwood sourcing; look for FSC-certified stock.
  • Balsa—extremely low density (as low as 100–200 kg/m³), making it the lightest commercial timber. Used for model making and structural cores in composite panels (e.g. wind turbine blades). Despite its softness, it has a high strength-to-weight ratio.
  • Jelutong—a fine-grained, uniform hardwood widely used in D&T education for model making and pattern carving. It is easy to cut, sand and shape accurately, making it ideal for producing prototypes and moulding patterns.

Named Softwoods

  • Scots pine—a widely available European softwood used for structural timber, joinery and furniture. It has a pale yellow colour with distinct resin pockets. Moderately strong and easy to work.
  • Western red cedar—a naturally durable softwood with high rot resistance due to its phenolic oils. Used for exterior cladding, garden furniture and roof shingles without needing chemical treatment. Has a distinctive reddish-brown colour and pleasant aroma.
  • Parana pine—a fine-grained softwood from South America, unusual in softwoods for being relatively knot-free. Used in high-quality interior joinery, staircases and shelving where a clean appearance is needed. Its limited availability has made it more expensive than other softwoods.
Key Fact

Western red cedar’s natural durability comes from its phenolic oils, not a chemical preservative treatment—making it an environmentally preferred choice for exterior use. Jelutong is the standard studio modelling timber in D&T because it machines and carves accurately.

Manufactured Boards

Manufactured boards are engineered sheet materials. They eliminate many of the defects of solid timber and are available in large, consistent sheets (typically 2440 × 1220 mm). Key types:

  • Plywood—layers of veneer bonded with adjacent grains at 90° to each other. This cross-grain construction gives high strength in all directions and resistance to splitting. Structural grades (e.g. WBP—water and boil proof) are used in construction; decorative grades use hardwood face veneers.
  • MDF (medium-density fibreboard)—fine wood fibres bonded with synthetic resin under heat and pressure. Produces a uniform, smooth surface with no grain, which takes paint and veneers extremely well. However, MDF is heavy, absorbs moisture at edges and cannot be used structurally where loads must be resisted.
  • Chipboard (particleboard)—compressed wood chips bonded with adhesive. Cheaper than MDF or plywood; commonly used in flat-pack furniture (often surfaced with a melamine laminate). Weak at the edges and screws do not hold as well as in solid timber.
  • Hardboard—a thin, dense sheet made from wood pulp fibres compressed under steam and heat. One face is smooth, the other textured. Used for drawer bases, backs of furniture and low-cost panels.

Natural timber contains inherent defects that affect quality and strength. Common defects include:

  • Knots—where branches once grew. Knots disrupt the grain, weaken the timber at that point and can shrink and fall out over time. Structural timber grades limit knot size and position.
  • Shrinkage and warping—timber continues to absorb and release moisture after felling. Uneven drying causes cupping (edges curl up), bowing (along the length) and twisting. Kiln-drying reduces but does not eliminate movement.
  • Shakes—cracks that run along the grain. Ring shakes follow the annual growth rings; star shakes radiate outward from the centre. Both weaken the board and may open further as the timber dries.
  • Fungal attack—wet rot and dry rot fungi degrade wood fibres if timber remains damp. Preservative treatment (e.g. pressure impregnation with copper-based compounds) is used for outdoor structural timber.

Manufactured boards overcome most of these defects because the manufacturing process eliminates directional grain dependence, large knots and growth-related stresses. This is a key advantage when selecting sheet material for flat furniture components.

Finishing timber protects it from moisture, UV light and physical wear, and enhances appearance. Common finishes include:

  • Varnish—a clear resin coating that cures to a hard, durable surface. Polyurethane varnish is water-resistant and tough, suitable for floors and furniture. Satin and gloss sheens are available.
  • Stain—penetrates the timber fibres to change colour without hiding grain. Oil-based stains are absorbed deeply; water-based stains raise the grain slightly but have lower VOC emissions.
  • Paint—fully opaque finish that hides grain. Requires a primer coat on bare wood to seal the surface and improve adhesion. Suitable for MDF (which does not have a visible grain) and exterior joinery.
  • Danish oil / linseed oil—penetrating oils that soak into the wood fibres, feeding the timber and giving a natural, low-sheen appearance. Often used on hardwoods where the grain is intended to be visible. Requires periodic reapplication.

Ferrous vs Non-Ferrous

Metals are divided into two fundamental categories. Ferrous metals contain iron. They are generally strong and magnetic, but rust when exposed to moisture and oxygen unless protected. Non-ferrous metals contain no iron. They resist corrosion naturally and are non-magnetic—making them valuable in electrical applications (where magnetic interference must be avoided) and in marine environments. The third category, alloys, are mixtures of two or more metals (or a metal and another element) engineered to achieve properties neither constituent has alone.

Key Fact

Ferrous metals contain iron and tend to rust; non-ferrous metals do not contain iron and resist corrosion naturally. Mild steel (ferrous) and aluminium (non-ferrous) are the most commonly used metals in manufacturing industry.

Ferrous Metals — Named Examples

Cast iron contains 2–4% carbon, making it very hard and brittle. It cannot be bent or forged—it fractures rather than deforming. Used for machine tool beds, drain covers and engine blocks, where rigidity under compression is needed and brittleness is acceptable. It has excellent compressive strength but low tensile strength.

Mild steel (also called low-carbon steel) contains 0.1–0.3% carbon. It is the most widely used engineering material in the world. Tensile strength is approximately 400–500 MPa. It is ductile, malleable and weldable—but rusts readily and must be painted, galvanised or powder-coated for outdoor use. Used in structural beams, car bodies, pipework and general fabrication.

Medium and high carbon steels have progressively more carbon (0.3–1.4%), giving greater hardness and wear resistance but reduced ductility and weldability. High carbon steel is used for cutting tools, springs and high-stress components. It can be heat-treated (hardened and tempered) to control the balance of hardness and toughness.

Non-Ferrous Metals — Named Examples

Aluminium has a density of approximately 2.7 g/cm³—about one third the density of steel. It naturally forms an oxide layer that prevents further corrosion. Good conductor of heat and electricity. Used in aircraft frames, food cans, window frames and heat exchangers. Can be anodised to enhance its oxide layer and add colour. Recycling aluminium uses only around 5% of the energy needed to smelt virgin aluminium from bauxite.

Copper is an excellent electrical conductor (second only to silver) and has high thermal conductivity. It is ductile enough to be drawn into fine wire and malleable enough to be beaten into shape. Used in electrical wiring, plumbing pipes and heat exchangers. Copper weathers to a green patina (copper carbonate) that actually protects the underlying metal.

Common Alloys

Alloys are engineered mixtures. The specification names brass and bronze specifically:

  • Brass—copper (roughly 65%) and zinc (roughly 35%). Harder than copper alone, non-sparking, and corrosion-resistant. Used in musical instruments, plumbing fittings, electrical connectors and decorative hardware. Machines cleanly with a good surface finish.
  • Bronze—copper and tin (historically around 88% copper, 12% tin). Harder and more corrosion-resistant than copper alone. Used in bearings, marine propellers, bells and sculpture. The tin content makes it harder to machine than brass but gives superior strength for load-bearing applications.
Key Fact

Brass = copper + zinc. Bronze = copper + tin. Both are corrosion-resistant alloys derived from copper. Brass is commonly used for plumbing fittings and musical instruments; bronze for marine propellers and bearings.

Working Properties

Designers and engineers select metals based on specific working properties. These are the key terms the exam tests:

PropertyDefinitionHigh-value example
Tensile strengthResist pulling forcesMild steel (~400–500 MPa)
HardnessResist surface indentation or scratchingHigh carbon steel
DuctilityDrawn into wireCopper, aluminium
MalleabilityBeaten or pressed into shape without crackingAluminium, copper
ToughnessAbsorb impact energy without fracturingMild steel
ElasticityReturn to original shape after load removedSpring steel

Metals are supplied in standard stock forms to minimise waste when cutting components to size. Common forms include:

  • Sheet—flat rolled metal, typically 0.5–3 mm thick for mild steel and aluminium. Used for pressed body panels, enclosures and cans.
  • Bar (flat/square)—solid rectangular or square cross-section. Used for structural brackets, levers and frames.
  • Rod (round bar)—solid circular cross-section, turned in a lathe to produce shafts and pins.
  • Tube—hollow circular section. High strength-to-weight ratio because material is placed at maximum distance from the neutral axis. Used for cycle frames, scaffold poles and handrails.
  • Angle—L-shaped cross-section. Provides stiffness to a structure when welded or bolted at corners. Used in frames, brackets and shelving.

Ferrous metals must be protected from moisture and oxygen to prevent rust. Common methods include:

  • Galvanising—dipping steel in molten zinc. The zinc acts as a sacrificial coating: it corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel beneath. Used for outdoor structures, car body panels undercoating and corrugated roofing.
  • Powder coating—electrostatically applying a dry polymer powder to a metal surface, then curing it in an oven. Produces a hard, even coating in a wide range of colours. More durable than conventional liquid paint and produces less VOC waste.
  • Painting—the simplest surface treatment. Requires proper surface preparation (degreasing, priming) to adhere well. Relatively low cost but needs re-application as the paint chips or weathers.
  • Anodising (aluminium)—an electrochemical process that thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminium. The thickened layer is then dyed. Produces a decorative and very wear-resistant surface. Used on window frames, bicycle components and consumer electronics.

Polymers in the Modern World

Polymers are ubiquitous in modern product design—from food packaging to aircraft interiors. All polymers share the same fundamental structure: long molecular chains of repeated units called monomers. The critical distinction for designers and engineers is whether the polymer can be re-melted and reformed (thermoforming) or whether it permanently sets on first cure (thermosetting). This determines which manufacturing processes can be used and how the product performs under heat in service.

Thermoforming Polymers (Thermoplastics)

Thermoforming polymers (also called thermoplastics) soften when heated and become rigid again on cooling. This cycle can be repeated many times without degradation of the molecular chains. This makes them recyclable and processable by injection moulding, vacuum forming, blow moulding and extrusion. The most widely used thermoforming polymers are:

  • Polythene (polyethylene, PE)—available in two main grades. High-density polyethylene (HDPE) has a melting point of approximately 130°C and is stiff, hard and chemical-resistant. Used for milk bottles, bottle caps and pipes. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) is softer and more flexible—used for plastic bags and squeeze bottles. Both are readily recyclable (HDPE is recycling code 2; LDPE is code 4).
  • Polypropylene (PP)—a tough, semi-rigid polymer with excellent chemical resistance and a high melting point (~160–170°C). Its “living hinge” property (thin sections can be flexed repeatedly without cracking) makes it ideal for flip-top bottle caps, food containers and battery cases. Lightweight: density approximately 0.9 g/cm³, which means it floats in water.
  • Polystyrene (PS)—in its standard form, a rigid, brittle, clear polymer used for CD cases and model kits. Expanded polystyrene (EPS) is the white foam used in packaging and disposable coffee cups. High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) blends rubber to improve toughness and is used for refrigerator liners and display models.
  • PVC (polyvinyl chloride)—one of the most versatile polymers: rigid PVC is used for window frames, guttering and drainage pipes; plasticised PVC (with added plasticisers to increase flexibility) is used for electrical cable insulation, flooring and inflatable products. PVC is durable and weather-resistant but raises environmental concerns because chlorine-based additives can form toxic compounds at end-of-life incineration.
Key Fact

Thermoforming polymers soften on heating and can be recycled—making them suitable for injection moulding and vacuum forming. HDPE melts at ~130°C; polypropylene at ~160–170°C. Polypropylene’s “living hinge” property (repeated flexing without cracking) is unique among common polymers.

Thermosetting Polymers

Thermosetting polymers undergo a permanent chemical change when first cured. Cross-links form between the molecular chains, creating a rigid three-dimensional network. Once set, they cannot be re-melted or recycled—heating them too strongly causes charring and degradation rather than softening. This makes them extremely heat-resistant in service, which is why they are used in electrical fittings, worktops and adhesives. The four named thermosets in the specification are:

  • Urea formaldehyde (UF)—a white or coloured rigid thermoset. Used for electrical fittings (plug casings, light switch covers) and white bottle caps. Good surface hardness and electrical insulation. Brittle compared with thermoplastics.
  • Melamine formaldehyde (MF)—harder and more heat- and stain-resistant than UF. Used to surface kitchen worktops (Formica is a trade name for MF-laminated board), crockery and the surfaces of MDF and chipboard in furniture. The high surface hardness resists scratching from utensils.
  • Polyester resin (PR)—a liquid that cures with a catalyst (usually MEKP). Used in fibreglass (GRP) boat hulls and car body repair. When reinforced with glass fibre it produces a composite with good strength-to-weight ratio. Low viscosity makes it easy to apply by hand lay-up or resin infusion.
  • Epoxy resin (ER)—a two-part system (resin + hardener) that cures to a very strong, chemical-resistant material. Used in high-performance composites (e.g. carbon fibre reinforced polymer in aerospace components), as a structural adhesive (Araldite is a consumer epoxy adhesive) and as a protective coating. Stronger and more versatile than polyester resin but significantly more expensive.
Key Fact

The four thermosetting polymers to know are: urea formaldehyde (UF) — electrical fittings; melamine formaldehyde (MF) — kitchen worktop surfaces; polyester resin (PR) — fibreglass boat hulls; epoxy resin (ER) — high-performance composites and structural adhesives. None can be recycled by re-melting.

A key exam skill is comparing the two polymer types directly. This table summarises the differences:

PropertyThermoformingThermosetting
Behaviour on heatingSoftens and can be reshapedChars/degrades; cannot be softened
Molecular structureLinear or branched chainsCross-linked 3D network
RecyclabilityRecyclable (re-melt)Not recyclable by heat
Heat resistance in serviceLimited by softening pointExcellent — used near heat sources
Typical processingInjection moulding, vacuum forming, extrusionCompression moulding, hand lay-up, casting with catalyst
ExamplePolypropylene (PP)Urea formaldehyde (UF)

Examiner data shows that very few students choose polymers as their Q6 material, and those who do often rely on generic statements like “plastics are lightweight and cheap.” Stronger answers go beyond the obvious “PET bottle” examples and demonstrate breadth:

  • Name two or more specific polymers with their full names (e.g. “polypropylene” not “plastic”).
  • Link properties to mechanism: “polypropylene’s living hinge property means thin sections can flex thousands of times without cracking—unlike most polymers—making it ideal for flip-top caps.”
  • Include a thermoset example: epoxy resin or melamine formaldehyde in a kitchen worktop context shows you know both categories.
  • Address sustainability: thermoforming polymers can be recycled by re-melting; thermosetting polymers cannot be melted and are more challenging to recover at end of life.

Where Fibres Come From

Every textile begins with a fibre. Fibres are classified by their origin: natural fibres come from animals, insects or plants; synthetic fibres are manufactured from petrochemical or cellulose-based polymers. Understanding the source of a fibre is the first step in predicting its properties—animal and insect fibres have a protein structure; plant fibres have a cellulose structure; synthetic fibres are engineered, which means their properties can be designed for a specific performance target.

Animal and Insect Fibres

Animal and insect fibres are protein-based. The primary animal fibres the specification names are:

  • Wool—from sheep. The microscopic scales on each wool fibre interlock when agitated in warm water, causing shrinkage and felting. Wool is naturally fire-resistant (it chars rather than melts and self-extinguishes), an excellent insulator, and absorbs up to 30% of its weight in moisture vapour before feeling wet. Used in knitwear, suits and blankets.
  • Cashmere—from the fine undercoat of Kashmiri goats. Exceptionally soft and lightweight, with superior insulating properties. Significantly more expensive than standard wool due to the small yield per animal (typically 150–200 g per goat per year). Used in luxury knitwear and scarves.
  • Mohair—from Angora goats. Long, lustrous, fine fibres with a silky appearance and high sheen. Resilient (springs back quickly) and durable compared with other luxury fibres. Used in high-end knitwear, suiting and upholstery.
  • Angora—from Angora rabbits (not goats; the name is shared but the animal differs). Extremely fine, lightweight and fluffy. Poorly resilient—the fibres tend to shed and pill with wear. Often blended with wool to improve durability while retaining softness.
  • Alpaca—from alpacas. Similar to wool in structure but lacks the irritating scales that cause wool to feel scratchy against sensitive skin. Hypoallergenic, warm and lustrous. Used in outdoor clothing and knitwear.
  • Silk—from the cocoon of the silkworm (Bombyx mori). The silkworm spins a continuous filament up to 900 metres long. Silk is strong, lustrous, naturally temperature-regulating (warm in cool conditions, cool in warm conditions) and extremely fine. Used in luxury clothing, ties and parachute fabric historically. High cost reflects the labour-intensive reeling process.
Key Fact

Silk comes from the continuous filament cocoon of the silkworm (Bombyx mori) and is one of the strongest natural fibres. Wool is naturally fire-resistant because its protein structure (keratin) chars rather than melts and self-extinguishes. Cashmere comes from the undercoat of Kashmiri goats.

Plant Fibres

Plant fibres are cellulose-based and include:

  • Cotton—from the seed pod of the cotton plant. The most widely used natural fibre globally. Soft, breathable and highly absorbent (can hold up to 27 times its weight in water). Cotton is easy to wash and dye. Weaknesses: low elasticity (it creases easily), shrinks in hot water, and conventional cotton farming uses large amounts of pesticides and water. Organic cotton addresses some environmental concerns.
  • Linen (flax)—from the stem of the flax plant. Stronger than cotton when wet, with low elasticity (prone to creasing). Naturally cool to the touch because of its high thermal conductivity. Used in summer clothing, tablecloths and bedding.
  • Hemp—from the cannabis plant stem. Very strong and durable with natural antibacterial properties. Requires minimal pesticides. Coarser than cotton but becoming increasingly popular in sustainable fashion as processing techniques improve.
  • Jute—a coarse plant fibre used for sacking, hessian and rope. Biodegradable and inexpensive, but low durability in comparison to other natural fibres.

Regenerated and Synthetic Fibres

Rayon / viscose—regenerated fibres made by dissolving cellulose (wood pulp) and extruding it through fine holes to form filaments. Viscose has a soft, silky feel and drapes well. It is not synthetic in the strict sense (the raw material is natural cellulose) but the manufacturing process is wholly industrial. Tencel (Lyocell) is a more environmentally responsible regenerated cellulose fibre—the closed-loop Lyocell process recovers over 99% of the solvent, making it significantly more sustainable than conventional viscose.

Fully synthetic fibres are manufactured from petrochemical polymers:

  • Polyester—the most widely used synthetic fibre. Strong, quick-drying, wrinkle-resistant and retains shape well. Low moisture absorption (dries quickly but may feel clammy in hot conditions). Used in outdoor clothing, sportswear and most woven fabrics in blended yarns.
  • Nylon—the first fully synthetic fibre. Extremely strong and abrasion-resistant. Used in hosiery, ropes, parachutes and sportswear. Low moisture absorption.
  • Acrylic—designed to mimic wool. Lightweight, warm and soft. Less expensive than wool; machine washable. Weaker wet strength and pills more readily than wool. Used in knitwear, fleece and craft yarn.
  • Elastane (Lycra)—a segmented polyurethane fibre with exceptional elasticity—it can stretch up to five times its resting length and fully recover. Always used blended (typically 2–20% in a fabric) because pure elastane fabric does not hold shape. Used in sportswear, swimwear and stretch denim.
  • Aramid—a high-performance synthetic (e.g. Kevlar and Nomex). Extremely high tensile strength and heat resistance. Used in body armour, fire-protective clothing and aerospace applications. Far more expensive than everyday synthetics.
  • Tactel—a branded form of nylon microfibre developed by Invista. Softer, lighter and more breathable than standard nylon. Used in sportswear, lingerie and outdoor technical clothing.
Key Fact

The specification names two branded fibres explicitly: Tactel is a branded nylon microfibre (softer and more breathable than standard nylon) used in sportswear; Tencel is a branded lyocell regenerated cellulose fibre produced in a closed-loop process that recovers 99%+ of solvent, making it highly sustainable.

A blended fibre mixes two or more different fibre types in the same yarn (e.g. 80% cotton / 20% polyester). A mixed fabric combines different yarns in the same weave (e.g. a cotton warp with a polyester weft). The difference matters for labelling and recycling—blended yarns are impossible to separate, making end-of-life fibre recovery very difficult.

Common blending rationale:

  • Cotton + polyester: cotton’s softness and breathability + polyester’s strength and wrinkle resistance. Standard in shirts and workwear.
  • Wool + acrylic: wool’s warmth and natural feel + acrylic’s lower cost and machine-washability. Common in affordable knitwear.
  • Angora + wool: angora’s extreme softness + wool’s durability (angora fibres shed readily on their own). Used in luxury knitwear.

Exam questions may ask you to compare fibre properties for a specific product. Properties to know:

PropertyHigh exampleLow example
StrengthNylon, silk, aramidAngora, cotton (wet)
ElasticityElastane (Lycra)Cotton, linen
AbsorbencyCotton (27× its weight), woolNylon, polyester
InsulationCashmere, woolCotton, linen (cool feel)
DurabilityNylon, polyester, aramidAngora, low-grade viscose
FlammabilityCotton (burns readily)Wool (self-extinguishes)

lesson_title: Woven, Non-Woven and Knitted Textile Construction
content_html:
From Fibre to Fabric

Choosing the right fibre is only the beginning. The way fibres are assembled into a fabric structure determines how the final textile performs—its strength, drape, stretch, durability and appearance. Three major construction methods exist: weaving (interlacing two sets of yarns at right angles), knitting (looping a single yarn into interlocking stitches) and non-woven processes (bonding fibres directly into a sheet without spinning or weaving). Each gives a different combination of properties.

Woven Fabrics

Weaving interlaces two sets of yarn. The yarn running lengthways on the loom is the warp; the yarn running crossways (inserted by a shuttle or rapier on each pass) is the weft. The pattern of interlacing determines the weave structure. The three fundamental weaves are:

Plain weave is the most basic and most common construction. The weft passes over one warp thread and under the next, reversing on the following row. This produces a symmetrical, grid-like pattern that is the same on both sides. It has the most interlacement points of any weave, which gives it:

  • High durability—many interlacement points mean yarns are held firmly.
  • Low drape—the firm structure does not hang or flow easily.
  • Tendency to fray—cut edges must be finished or seamed.

Examples: cotton calico, muslin, taffeta, canvas. Used in shirts, bags, sails and base fabrics for printing.

Twill weave passes the weft over two (or more) warp threads before going under one, shifting by one thread on each row. This creates the characteristic diagonal rib line visible on the fabric surface. Properties:

  • Better drape than plain weave—fewer interlacement points allow yarns to move more freely.
  • Good abrasion resistance—the diagonal rib distributes friction across a larger yarn area.
  • Can be woven more tightly—so it can be heavier and more windproof than plain weave at the same yarn count.

Examples: denim (2/1 twill with indigo-dyed warp), herringbone, gabardine. Used in jeans, suits, uniforms and upholstery.

Satin weave has warp threads floating over four or more weft threads before interlacing. The very few interlacement points mean long yarn floats lie flat on the surface, creating the fabric’s characteristic smooth, high-sheen appearance. Properties:

  • Excellent drape—minimal interlacement allows the fabric to hang fluidly.
  • Lustrous surface—long yarn floats reflect light uniformly.
  • Snagging risk—long floating yarns catch easily on rough surfaces.
  • Distinct face and back—the two surfaces look very different.

Examples: silk satin, polyester satin, sateen (using cotton). Used in eveningwear, linings, bedding and parachute fabric.

Key Fact

Plain weave has the most interlacement points—making it the most durable but with the least drape. Twill weave has a diagonal rib; it drapes better and resists abrasion well (hence denim). Satin weave has long yarn floats creating a lustrous surface with excellent drape but a snagging risk.

Non-Woven Fabrics

Non-woven fabrics are produced without spinning or weaving. Fibres are laid as a web and bonded together by one of three methods: mechanical entanglement (needle-punching or hydroentangling), thermal bonding (melting a proportion of synthetic fibres to fuse the web) or chemical bonding (applying an adhesive binder).

  • Felt—produced by applying heat, moisture and mechanical pressure to wool or other protein fibres. The microscopic scales on wool fibres interlock and mat together permanently. Felt does not fray when cut (because there is no woven structure to unravel), making it easy to cut to shape for craft, padding, and industrial gaskets. However, it has low tensile strength compared with woven fabrics.
  • Bonded fabrics—include interfacing used in garment construction (fusible interfacing is bonded to the wrong side of a fabric with heat to add stiffness), geotextiles used in civil engineering for soil stabilisation and drainage, and medical non-wovens (disposable gowns, masks) where single-use hygiene is prioritised over durability.

Knitted Fabrics

Knitting uses a single yarn looped into interlocking stitches. The two main types are:

  • Weft knit—the yarn runs horizontally across the fabric. Stitches in a row interlock with those in the row below. Weft knit fabric stretches easily in both directions and is comfortable against skin. It also ladders—if a stitch breaks, the column can unravel downward. Used in T-shirts, underwear, socks and casual knitwear. Can be produced on circular or flat-bed knitting machines at high speed.
  • Warp knit—multiple yarns run simultaneously in the warp (lengthways) direction, each forming loops that interlock with adjacent yarns on each course. The fabric is much more stable dimensionally than weft knit—it does not ladder easily. Used in lingerie, swimwear linings, velvet backing and sports mesh. Generally produced on specialist Raschel or Tricot machines.
Key Fact

Weft knit runs the yarn horizontally; it stretches comfortably but can ladder if a stitch breaks. Warp knit uses multiple yarns running vertically and interlocking sideways; it is dimensionally stable and does not ladder, making it suitable for swimwear and lingerie linings.

Twill weaveLowMediumHighYesDenim, suits
Satin weaveLowHighMediumYes (floats snag)Eveningwear, linings
Felt (non-woven)LowLowLowNoneCraft, gaskets, padding
