lesson_title: Context, User Needs and Design Briefs
content_html:
Starting with Context

Every design project begins with a context. A context might be a social problem (increasing food waste at home), a commercial opportunity (a gap in the market for portable water filtration), or a specific environment (designing furniture for a hospital ward). Before any ideas are sketched, designers must understand the context thoroughly — who is affected, what they need, and what constraints exist.

Understanding context involves identifying the end user — not just anyone who might buy the product, but the specific group whose life will be improved by it. A wheelchair designed without input from wheelchair users will almost certainly fail in ways a desk-based designer could never anticipate. This is why designers spend time gathering evidence before they generate ideas.

Key Fact

Designers use two types of research: primary research (gathered first-hand from users and the environment) and secondary research (gathered from existing sources such as books, websites and reports). Both types inform the design brief and specification.

Primary Research Methods

Primary research involves direct contact with users or the context being designed for. Common methods include:

  • Questionnaires and surveys — gather opinions from a large number of people quickly. Closed questions (yes/no, rating scales) are easy to analyse; open questions give richer, qualitative detail.
  • Interviews — allow deeper conversation with individual users. A designer working on a mobility aid might interview physiotherapists and patients to understand specific difficulties with existing products.
  • Observation — watching users interact with existing products in their real environment. This often reveals problems users cannot articulate themselves.
  • Analysis of existing products (disassembly) — breaking down a competitor product to understand how it is made, what materials are used, and where it succeeds or fails.

Secondary Research Methods

Secondary research draws on information already collected by others. Sources include market reports, published statistics, existing product reviews, manufacturer data sheets, and academic studies. Secondary research is faster and cheaper than primary research but may be less specific to the exact context. Designers use it to establish background understanding before conducting primary investigation.

Product analysis is a key primary research skill. When designers examine an existing product, they consider function (does it work as intended?), aesthetics (does it appeal to users?), materials (are the right materials used for the application?), manufacturing processes (how was it made and at what cost?), ergonomics (does it fit human dimensions and movement?), and sustainability (how long will it last, can it be recycled or repaired?).

This structured approach — sometimes called ACCESS FM (Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Safety, Size, Function, Materials) — helps designers avoid reinventing the wheel and identify genuine improvement opportunities in the market.

The Design Brief

Once the context and user needs are understood, the designer or client produces a design brief. A good brief is concise and open-ended. It identifies the problem to be solved and the intended user, but deliberately avoids prescribing the solution — that is left for the design process to discover.

For example, a brief might read: “Design a product to help older adults living independently to manage their daily medication accurately and safely.” This tells the designer who the user is and what the problem is, but does not say whether the solution should be a physical dispenser, a digital reminder system, or a combination of both. The brief keeps options open.

Key Fact

A design brief states the problem. A design specification turns that problem into measurable criteria that the final product must meet. The brief comes first; the specification is developed once research is complete.

Writing a Design Specification

A design specification translates the brief into testable requirements. Each point should be precise and measurable. Vague statements like “the product should be comfortable” are less useful than “the handle diameter must fall within 30–45 mm to suit the 5th–95th percentile adult grip.”

Specification points typically cover areas such as:

  • Function — what the product must do and how well it must do it.
  • User needs — size, weight, ease of use, accessibility requirements.
  • Safety — standards the product must meet (e.g. CE marking for electrical products).
  • Materials and manufacturing — constraints imposed by the production method or budget.
  • Aesthetics — visual style that will appeal to the target user.
  • Sustainability — specific actions such as “must use at least 30% recycled material” rather than vague goals like “eco-friendly.”

Examiners consistently reward specific, measurable specification points and penalise vague ones. Compare these two examples for a children’s cup:

Vague (weak): “The cup should be safe for children.”
Specific (strong): “The cup must be made from food-grade, BPA-free polymer and have no components smaller than 45 mm in any direction to eliminate choking risk.”

The same principle applies to sustainability requirements. “Make it more eco-friendly” scores no marks. “Use recycled high-density polyethylene (HDPE) for the outer shell” or “design for disassembly so components can be separated at end of life” are the types of response examiners credit.

How Brief and Specification Interact

In professional design practice, the brief and specification are living documents. As a design develops through prototyping and user testing, new information emerges that may lead to specification points being refined. For example, early user testing of a portable speaker might reveal that the grip depth assumed in the original specification is too narrow for users with larger hands — the specification is then updated before further development continues.

This iterative relationship between research, brief, specification and design is central to the design process. It reflects the real-world truth that good products are rarely designed in a single pass.

lesson_title: Investigating the Work of Designers and Companies
content_html:
Why Study Designers and Companies?

Examiners expect students to know how the work of specific designers and companies has shaped the products we use today. Studying these figures reveals how professional designers think — what problems they set out to solve, what values drive their decisions, and how their philosophy shows up in physical products. The five you need to know for your exam are Airbus, Apple, James Dyson, Philippe Starck, and Matthew Williamson.

Airbus — Engineering at Scale

Airbus represents large-scale engineering design. Its products are shaped by tight constraints: safety regulations, passenger capacity, fuel efficiency, and the physical limits of materials at altitude. Every element of an aircraft — from the wing profile to the seat foam density — is the result of iterative testing and compromise between competing demands.

The A380 is the most studied Airbus example for GCSE purposes. Designers faced the challenge of creating the world’s largest commercial passenger aircraft while meeting strict noise and fuel-consumption limits. Composite materials (carbon fibre reinforced polymer) replaced heavier aluminium in key structural sections, reducing weight without sacrificing strength. The wing design was optimised through thousands of hours of computer simulation and wind tunnel testing before a physical prototype was built.

Key Fact

Airbus design philosophy prioritises engineering precision over aesthetics. Key decisions — such as using composite materials in the A380’s wings to reduce weight and improve fuel efficiency — are driven by measurable performance data and safety regulations, not visual style.

Apple — Design as Differentiation

Under Jony Ive as Chief Design Officer, Apple developed a design philosophy built on simplicity, material quality, and the removal of unnecessary elements. Products like the iMac G3 (1998), the iPod (2001), and the iPhone (2007) succeeded partly because of their engineering but equally because of their visual and tactile identity.

Apple’s approach treats the exterior finish as part of the product’s communication to the user. The single-piece aluminium body of the MacBook, machined from a solid billet, signals durability and premium quality through material choice alone. Interface design is integrated with hardware: buttons are removed or minimised so the product’s form suggests its function. Apple also controls the manufacturing process closely — tolerances on machined aluminium parts are held to fractions of a millimetre.

When writing about Apple in an extended answer, focus on three linked ideas: minimalism (reduce elements to essentials), material precision (choice of material communicates brand values), and integration (hardware and software designed together). Examiners reward responses that connect design decisions to outcomes — e.g. “Removing the headphone jack from the iPhone reduced the number of components and waterproofing failure points, reflecting Apple’s philosophy of simplification even when this created short-term controversy.”

James Dyson — Problem-Led Innovation

James Dyson trained as a designer and became famous for solving a problem that manufacturers had accepted as unsolvable: vacuum cleaners losing suction as the dust bag fills. Dyson noticed that industrial cyclone separators — large centrifugal devices used in sawmills — separated particles from air without a bag. After reportedly over 5,000 prototype iterations across five years, the G-Force cyclonic vacuum cleaner was launched in 1983 in Japan before reaching the UK market in 1993 as the DC01.

Dyson’s design philosophy is defined by a willingness to rethink fundamentals rather than improve existing solutions incrementally. This is reflected in later products: a bladeless fan that uses the Coanda effect to amplify airflow, a hand dryer that removes water by forcing air across the hands at 430 mph rather than evaporating it with heat, and a robotic vacuum cleaner with a spinning brush that self-cleans. Each product is built around a single insight that makes a previous compromise unnecessary.

Key Fact

Dyson’s core philosophy is problem-led: identify a widely accepted compromise, find the underlying reason it exists, and then design a product that eliminates the compromise entirely. The bagless vacuum cleaner eliminated the accepted ‘loss of suction’ compromise through cyclonic separation.

Philippe Starck — Postmodern Playfulness

Philippe Starck is associated with postmodern design — work that is provocative, humorous, and deliberately challenges what an everyday object is expected to look like. His most studied product is the Juicy Salif citrus squeezer (1990, manufactured by Alessi). Starck designed it as a three-legged, spider-like object cast in aluminium. It is deliberately inefficient as a juicer — the juice splashes rather than being channelled — but it functions as a conversation piece and sculpture as much as a kitchen tool.

Starck’s philosophy argues that products should do more than their stated function: they should provoke thought, elicit emotion, and communicate something about their owner’s taste and values. He has applied this approach to furniture, architecture, toothbrushes and motorbikes. For the exam, the key idea is that Starck treats aesthetics as a primary function rather than a finishing consideration.

Matthew Williamson — Colour and Textile Identity

Matthew Williamson is a British fashion designer whose work is immediately recognisable through its bold use of colour and pattern. Where many fashion designers define themselves through silhouette or construction, Williamson’s signature is the surface: layered colour combinations inspired by travels in India and elsewhere, intricate printed patterns, and a palette that contrasts where other designers coordinate.

Williamson has collaborated with companies including Debenhams and Pucci, extending his visual language beyond clothing into homeware and interiors. For exam purposes, the important idea is that his design philosophy demonstrates how a visual identity — a consistent approach to colour, pattern and material — can become a commercial asset that translates across product categories.

Use this summary to compare the five in extended answers:

Designer/CompanyCore philosophyKey product
AirbusEngineering precision; performance data drives every decisionA380 aircraft
AppleMinimalism + material precision; form communicates functioniPhone, MacBook
DysonProblem-led innovation; eliminate accepted compromisesDC01 bagless vacuum
StarckPostmodern playfulness; aesthetics is a primary functionJuicy Salif squeezer
WilliamsonColour and pattern as commercial identity; cross-category translationFashion and homeware collections

lesson_title: Design Strategies and Avoiding Design Fixation
content_html:
What Is a Design Strategy?

A design strategy is the deliberate approach a designer or team takes to move from understanding a problem to finding a solution. Different strategies suit different types of problem. Some projects need deep collaboration between specialists; others require the designer to sit with users for days to understand their experience. Knowing which strategy to apply — and when to switch strategies — is a core professional skill.

User-Centred Design

User-centred design (UCD) treats the end user’s needs, behaviours, and limitations as the primary driver of every decision. Rather than starting from what can be manufactured or what the designer finds interesting, UCD begins with deep investigation of who will use the product and how they actually behave — not how the designer assumes they behave.

UCD relies on direct engagement with users throughout the process — not just at the start during research, but during prototyping and testing too. When a mobility-aid manufacturer involves wheelchair users in repeated rounds of testing, those users will consistently identify problems that engineers working from desk-based specifications would never anticipate. This is the core argument for UCD: it replaces assumption with evidence.

Key Fact

User-centred design keeps the end user’s real needs at the centre of every stage. It uses evidence gathered from direct contact with users — not assumptions — to drive design decisions, making it especially powerful for products used by vulnerable or specialist groups.

Collaborative Design

Collaborative design recognises that complex products cannot be designed by a single specialist. An aircraft requires aeronautical engineers, materials scientists, human factors specialists, software developers, and industrial designers. A medical device needs clinicians, regulatory experts, and manufacturing engineers. Collaboration means these specialists work together from the outset rather than handing a design from one department to the next.

The benefit of genuine collaboration (as opposed to sequential handover) is that conflicts between disciplines are identified and resolved early, when changes are cheap. If a software engineer only sees the hardware design after it is finalised, any interface conflict is expensive to fix. If both are in the room from the start, the interface is designed jointly.

Systems Thinking

Systems thinking treats a product not as an isolated object but as a component in a larger system. A smart thermostat is not just a device — it is part of a heating system, a home energy network, a user’s daily routine, a broadband connection, a smartphone app, and a supplier of data to an energy company. Designing the thermostat without considering these relationships will produce a product that works mechanically but fails in use.

Systems thinking also applies to sustainability. Designing a product in isolation from its supply chain, use context, and end-of-life disposal produces incomplete solutions. A packaging designer who considers only the structural brief — “protect the contents during transit” — without considering recycling infrastructure will design packaging that meets the brief but creates waste at scale.

The Double Diamond

The Double Diamond is a widely used model of the design process. It was developed by the Design Council and structures design into four phases: Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver. Each diamond represents a cycle of divergent thinking (opening up possibilities) followed by convergent thinking (narrowing down to a decision).

  • Discover — explore the problem widely. Conduct user research, observe contexts, gather evidence without filtering. The goal is breadth, not answers.
  • Define — analyse the research and synthesise a clear problem statement. This is where a design brief and specification emerge. The goal is to narrow understanding to the real problem.
  • Develop — generate a wide range of ideas and prototype solutions. Iteration happens here. The goal is breadth of potential solutions, tested against the specification.
  • Deliver — refine and test a chosen solution until it meets the specification. The goal is a final product or solution ready for production or use.
Key Fact

The Double Diamond has four phases: Discover (explore the problem), Define (clarify the real problem), Develop (generate and test solutions), Deliver (finalise and produce). Each pair of phases follows a diverge-then-converge pattern.

Design Fixation and How to Avoid It

Design fixation occurs when a designer becomes locked onto an early idea — their own or an existing product — and stops genuinely exploring alternatives. It is one of the most common barriers to creative design work. A designer who has seen a particular type of lamp will unconsciously replicate its form even when asked to design something completely new. The early idea becomes an invisible constraint.

Strategies designers use to break fixation include:

  • Random input — introducing an unrelated object or concept and forcing connections between it and the design problem. A lamp design session that starts with the random word “river” might generate forms based on flow, reflection, and meanders rather than conventional lamp shapes.
  • Reverse brainstorming — asking “how could we make this product worse?” or “what would cause this to fail?” and then reversing those answers to generate genuine improvements.
  • Analogous inspiration — looking at how a completely different sector has solved a similar problem. Hospital designers studying how Formula 1 pit stops achieve rapid, error-free team coordination found applications in surgical team handover processes.

Iterative design is the practice of repeatedly making, testing, and refining a product based on what testing reveals. Each cycle produces a better-informed design decision. James Dyson’s reported 5,000+ prototypes for the bagless vacuum cleaner is the most famous example: each failed version revealed a specific reason for failure that informed the next attempt.

Examiners reward extended responses on iterative design that show how user feedback informs decisions throughout the process — not just at the end. A response that says “we tested the prototype and improved it” is weaker than one that says “user testing revealed that the grip diameter was too large for users with small hands, so the handle was reduced from 45 mm to 32 mm before the next prototype was built.”

Students often list design strategy names without explaining what they involve or why they are appropriate for a given scenario. Writing “the designer used user-centred design” earns one mark at best. Writing “the designer used user-centred design because the product was intended for elderly users with limited mobility — assumptions about grip strength and reading distance would have led to design errors that only direct testing with the target group could prevent” earns the application marks that lift a response into the higher band.

Why Communication Is a Core Design Skill

A brilliant idea that cannot be communicated clearly will not become a product. Designers use a wide range of visual techniques — from rapid freehand sketches to precise engineering drawings — to share ideas with colleagues, clients, manufacturers, and users. Different audiences need different levels of detail: a client needs to understand what a product will look like; a factory worker needs to know exact dimensions, tolerances, and assembly sequence.

Understanding which communication method to choose in a given situation is itself a design decision. Choosing a quick annotated sketch during early ideation is appropriate; submitting a quick sketch to a manufacturer instead of a fully dimensioned working drawing would cause production errors.

Freehand Sketching and Annotated Sketches

Freehand sketching is the fastest way to externalise an idea. It does not need to be accurate to scale — its purpose is to communicate a concept quickly to allow evaluation and discussion. Annotated sketches add written notes to drawings to explain what cannot be communicated visually: the material, the surface finish, the reason a particular form was chosen, or a dimension that must be met for the product to function correctly.

In professional practice, designers often fill sketchbooks with annotated ideas during the early stages of a project. These sketches are not drafts of final products — they are thinking tools. The act of drawing forces the designer to make implicit ideas explicit and exposes problems that were not apparent when the idea existed only as a thought.

Key Fact

Designers use three main 3D drawing types: isometric (parallel projection, no vanishing point, accurate proportions), one-point perspective (one vanishing point, suited to interior spaces), and two-point perspective (two vanishing points, more realistic representation of exteriors and products).

2D Drawing Techniques

Orthographic projection presents a product from three separate views: the front elevation, the side elevation, and the plan view (looking down from above). Each view is drawn to scale and fully dimensioned. Orthographic projection uses a standardised symbol — either first-angle or third-angle projection — to indicate which arrangement of views has been used.

Orthographic drawings do not try to look realistic; they are optimised for precision. A manufacturer reading an orthographic drawing can determine the exact shape of every surface, the diameter of every hole, and the thickness of every wall without any visual interpretation. This removes ambiguity.

3D Drawing Techniques

Isometric drawing presents a product in three dimensions with all parallel edges drawn at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Because there is no vanishing point, lines that are parallel in reality remain parallel in the drawing, and all edges are drawn to their true length. This makes isometric drawing both realistic enough to communicate form and accurate enough to check proportions.

Perspective drawing adds vanishing points — points on the horizon where parallel lines converge — to create the impression of depth as the human eye sees it. One-point perspective, where all horizontal lines recede to a single vanishing point, is effective for interiors and tunnel-like views. Two-point perspective, with separate vanishing points for each set of parallel horizontal lines, creates a more natural representation of product exteriors.

An exploded diagram shows the components of a product pulled apart along a central axis, so the viewer can see how all parts relate to each other and in what order they are assembled. Assembly instructions for flat-pack furniture and electronic devices use exploded diagrams extensively because they communicate assembly sequence without requiring language.

A schematic diagram uses standardised symbols to represent components in an electrical or mechanical system. It is not a realistic picture; it shows logical connections and relationships. A circuit diagram uses BSI-standard symbols for resistors, capacitors, LEDs, and switches — any qualified engineer reading the diagram will interpret the symbols the same way regardless of the physical layout of the actual circuit.

Key Fact

Choosing the right communication method depends on the audience and purpose. Annotated sketches suit early ideation; isometric and perspective drawings communicate 3D form to clients; orthographic drawings give manufacturers exact production data; exploded diagrams show assembly sequence; schematics represent system connections.

Physical Models

Physical models allow designers and users to assess a product’s form, proportion, and ergonomics in ways that drawings cannot. Card, foam, clay, 3D-printed plastic, and laser-cut acrylic are all used as modelling materials depending on the level of detail required. A low-fidelity foam model is adequate for checking that a handle fits a hand; a high-fidelity 3D-printed model is used to test assembly fit or surface finish appearance.

Physical models also reveal problems that drawings mask. A handle that looks proportionate in an isometric drawing may feel too large when held, or a gap between components that appears negligible on paper may allow moisture ingress when the product is tested in real conditions.

Computer-Aided Design (CAD) and Mathematical Modelling

CAD (Computer-Aided Design) enables designers to create precise 2D and 3D digital models that can be rotated, sectioned, modified, and shared instantly. Unlike paper drawings, CAD models can be updated in seconds when a dimension changes. CAD software can also simulate physical properties: a structural analysis tool can calculate whether a beam will buckle under a given load without building a physical prototype.

Mathematical modelling uses equations and simulations to predict how a design will behave. Fluid dynamics software predicts airflow around a vehicle body; finite element analysis (FEA) calculates stress distribution in a loaded component. These tools allow designers to eliminate failure modes before any physical material is cut or formed, reducing both development cost and material waste.

A flow diagram maps a sequence of steps or decisions, using standard shapes: rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions, ovals for start/end points. In a manufacturing context, a flow diagram shows the sequence of operations needed to produce a component (e.g. mark out → cut to length → drill → file → inspect). In a design context, flow diagrams also represent control logic for electronic systems: an automatic street lamp might be shown as a decision diamond (“Is ambient light below 50 lux?”) leading to a process box (“Switch lamp on”).

Flow diagrams are communication tools as much as planning tools. A production manager reading a manufacturing flow diagram can identify bottlenecks, parallel processes, and quality-check points without needing to understand the technical detail of each operation.

Why Designers Build Prototypes

A prototype is a test vehicle. Designers build prototypes not because they expect them to be perfect, but because physical and digital models reveal problems that drawings and calculations cannot. When a design exists only as a sketch or a CAD file, it is possible to miss details that become immediately obvious the moment someone holds or interacts with the product.

Prototypes range widely in fidelity. A low-fidelity prototype might be a rough card model made in an afternoon to check the proportions of a product or whether a handle fits a hand. A high-fidelity prototype is a near-production unit used in the final stages of testing — made from the correct materials, with working mechanisms, and used to gather final approval before tooling for manufacture. Both types serve a purpose; choosing the wrong fidelity wastes time and money.

Key Fact

Prototypes range from low-fidelity (rough models to test form or scale) to high-fidelity (near-production models to test function and finish). Lower fidelity is used earlier in the process when many ideas are still in play; higher fidelity is used later when a design is being finalised.

What Prototypes Are Used to Test

A well-designed test programme evaluates a prototype against the criteria in the design specification. Typical tests cover:

  • Fitness for purpose — does the product do what the brief requires? A waterproof case that lets water in after 30 minutes is not fit for purpose regardless of its appearance.
  • Functionality — do all mechanisms, controls, and components work correctly together? A folding mechanism that catches and jams fails a functionality test even if each individual part is dimensionally correct.
  • Marketability — does the product appeal to the intended user? User panels may assess aesthetic appeal, perceived quality, and willingness to purchase.
  • Safety — does the product meet relevant safety standards? Products for children must be tested against requirements such as choking-hazard rules (no component smaller than 45 mm in any direction for products intended for children under 3).

Ergonomics

Ergonomics is the science of making products fit people rather than expecting people to adapt to products. An ergonomically designed tool is shaped to match the natural movements of the human hand, wrist, and arm, reducing the force required and the risk of repetitive strain. Ergonomics considers not just physical dimensions but also cognitive factors: a control panel with too many buttons, inconsistently labelled, creates cognitive overload and is ergonomically poor even if it is physically comfortable to touch.

When testing ergonomics, designers observe users interacting with a prototype in realistic conditions. A torque wrench that is comfortable to hold during light use may cause wrist fatigue after 30 minutes of heavy use — only testing under realistic conditions reveals this.

Anthropometrics

Anthropometrics is the collection and use of human body measurement data. Designers use percentile tables to design for the range of users they expect to encounter. A product designed for the 50th percentile fits the average user but excludes half the population at each extreme. Designing for the 5th to 95th percentile range is standard practice — this ensures the product works for 90% of the expected user population.

Common anthropometric measurements used in product design include hand grip span, finger length, shoulder width, eye height (standing and seated), reach distance, and foot length. Seat heights, door handle positions, keyboard dimensions, and steering wheel diameters are all derived from anthropometric data.

Key Fact

Designing for the 5th to 95th percentile means the product works for 90% of the expected user population. Designing only for the average (50th percentile) user excludes 50% of users at the taller, shorter, larger, or smaller extremes of the population range.

Testing and Feedback

User testing generates feedback that designers use to make informed decisions about changes. Effective user testing uses structured methods: task-based testing (asking a user to perform a specific action and observing where they struggle), think-aloud protocols (asking the user to describe what they are thinking while using the prototype), and rating scales (asking users to score specific attributes such as comfort, clarity, and visual appeal).

Examiners expect students to understand that feedback from user testing informs design decisions throughout the process, not just at the final stage. A designer who tests only a finished prototype and then modifies it is doing less effective design than one who tests a low-fidelity model early, identifies a structural problem, and revises the specification before any expensive materials are committed.

Iterative design follows a cycle: build → test → evaluate findings → modify → build again. Each cycle produces a design that is better informed than the previous version. The cycle continues until the product meets all specification criteria or until time and budget constraints require a decision to proceed with the best available version.

The key distinction examiners look for is whether feedback genuinely informs decisions or merely documents what happened. A strong response identifies a specific finding from testing (e.g. “users with small hands found the grip diameter of 45 mm caused fatigue after 10 minutes”), the decision it triggered (“the grip diameter was reduced to 32 mm and a softer thermoplastic elastomer grip was added”), and how the next test confirmed the change worked. Feedback that does not change anything is not iterative design — it is observation.

Critical Analysis and Evaluation

Critical analysis of a design means systematically assessing how well it meets each specification criterion, identifying where it falls short, and explaining what evidence supports that judgement. Examiners reward evaluations that are specific and evidence-based. “The handle was comfortable” is not an evaluation; “seven out of eight test users rated handle comfort above 4 out of 5, but the one user with smaller hands rated it 2, suggesting the lower grip limit should be reduced” is an evaluation.

Good evaluation also considers fitness for purpose holistically — a product may pass every individual specification test but still fail to feel right in use, because real use reveals interactions between criteria that individual tests do not capture.

Examiners have identified a recurring error: students describe user testing as useful only because it “improves the final product.” This misses half the mark. The examiner-rewarded point is that feedback from user testing informs design decisions throughout the iterative process — changing the specification, modifying the approach, and redirecting resources before expensive commitments are made. A response that shows testing changing an early prototype specification is stronger than one that shows testing polishing a nearly-finished product.
